implementation_notes: The functional Scala idiom adapts a type to an expected interface without touching either side: define the target trait as a typeclass and provide a `given` instance that implements it in terms of the existing type, exposing helper syntax through extension methods. The Scala documentation is explicit that extension methods replace what implicit classes and implicit conversions used to do, while conversions remain for genuine type-to-type coercions and require `scala.language.implicitConversions` (and warn on every use in Scala 3). The OO fallback is a delegating class implementing the target trait, which is what to use when the translation is stateful or the adapter must be a first-class value with its own identity.
pitfalls: Typeclass instances must be in implicit scope: a given defined in the wrong object or missing from the companion is invisible and the client reports 'no given instance' instead of finding your adapter.
Implicit conversions are never chained: Legacy -> Middle -> Target needs an explicit conversion step.
A Conversion does not make the adaptee a subtype for pattern matching, reflection or Java interop - code that inspects types still sees the adaptee.
Putting translation logic into an extension method makes it unavailable where only the typeclass instance can be summoned; keep the semantics in the instance and let extensions be syntax.

variants.name: Implicit conversion (legacy, Scala 2 style)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-Scala-3 way to let one type be used where another is expected is an implicit conversion - an implicit def in Scala 2 (normally defined in an object or package object), a `given Conversion[S, T]` in Scala 3. It makes the adaptee transparent at call sites: no wrapper value, no explicit adapt call, just a value of the wrong type where the right one is needed. That transparency is also the cost - conversions are silent and can fire anywhere - so the feature needs `import scala.language.implicitConversions`, warns on every use in Scala 3, and should be reserved for genuine coercions at library boundaries rather than used as a general adapter mechanism.
pitfalls: Conversion sites are invisible in the source: a value silently changes type, and activating a previously unused conversion can change behaviour during an unrelated refactor.
Two applicable conversions in scope make the call ambiguous, and the error appears at the use site rather than at the definition.
Conversions cannot add methods to a closed type - that is the job of extension methods; using Conversion for it produces surprising implicit materialisation.
Scala 3 keeps implicit defs only for compatibility; new code should define a Conversion instance so the intent is visible in the type.
